Note: the priority scheduling part will be divied into other PR and this pr only keeps session-aware tree cache and eviction policy.
In multi-turn inference scenarios (e.g., agentic workflows, RL rollouts), ongoing requests accumulate long cached prefixes across turns.
Under memory pressure, the standard radix cache may evict KV blocks without considering whether they are still referenced by active requests.
As a result, a new request can evict the cached prefix of an active multi-turn request even there are prefix caches that are not used by any requests, forcing full recomputation in the next turn and significantly reducing per-turn cache hit rates.

## Design
This PR introduces RefAwareCache, which adds per-node reference tracking and a three-tier eviction policy. The goal is to improve KV cache residency for active multi-turn requests, increase cache hit rates, and improve throughput under memory pressure.
RefAwareCache is also designed to work with priority-aware scheduling for better and flexiable scheduling policy in RL rollouts. In particular, low-priority requests are prevented from evicting KV cache entries that are referenced by in-flight high-priority requests.
This allows the scheduler to make more flexible admission and preemption decisions while preserving cache residency for important requests.
The radix cache eviction order is changed from a flat `evictable_leaves` policy to the following three-tier order:
TIER_UNUSED -> TIER_LOW_REF -> TIER_HIGH_REF
where:
TIER_UNUSED: nodes not used by any in-flight request
TIER_LOW_REF: nodes referenced only by low-priority requests
TIER_HIGH_REF: nodes referenced by at least one high-priority request
When eviction is needed, RefAwareCache evicts tokens following this tier order. Within the same tier, nodes with lower reference counts are evicted first.

### Motivation

## Motivating use case

Consider an RL system where we have a fixed set of K rollout workers, each of which runs 1 multi-turn rollout at a time with a max context length of N, and an sglang server which can fit T tokens in HiCache. In this scenario, we have at most K * N tokens of active context, so we hope to be able to scale K up to T / N while maintaining zero evictions of active context.

In reality, this does not happen, due to the following scenario:

Worker A starts rollout 1
Worker B starts and finishes rollout 1
Worker B starts and finishes rollout 2
Worker A finishes rollout 1

In this scenario, Worker A rollout 1 is pre-empted by up to 2 * N tokens. In general we see violations of the assumption that the rollout will be preempted by at most K * N tokens, and this causes cache misses which spiral into more cache misses. The issue is more severe for linear attention, since a rollout is pre-empted by a full Mamba state per request ().

## Why pinning, priority, and TTL are not enough

retention_seconds is implemented in https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/21045. However, in our example above:
* all rollouts are equal priority and should have equal TTL a priori
* we cannot know that worker B rollout 1 cache is stale until rollout 2 starts

Since we cannot proactively determine an appropriate TTL, we need to retroactively unpin or deprioritize previously cached requests as new requests are cached.

## Potential solutions

### Option A: retention slots

We may let the client specify a "retention_slot". Then any of the following would solve our problem, though with different behaviors in general:
* Option 1: Introduce an EvictionStrategy which first evicts nodes which are stale within their slot. We define staleness as follows: If there have been n requests within the retention_slot, and a node was last refreshed by the mth request within the slot, then the staleness is (n - m) within the slot. Hence, in our example above, as soon as Worker B starts making requests for rollout 2, its cache nodes from rollout 1 become stale, whereas Worker A's cache nodes are not stale despite being older.
* Option 2: Introduce an EvictionStrategy which first evicts from the retention_slot with the most tokens
* Option 3: Accept a retention_slot_size along with retention_slot. If inserting tokens under the retention_slot would exceed the retention_slot_size, evict tokens under the retention_slot.

Note:
* In all of these options, the case of nodes belonging to multiple slots needs to be handled
* Can be combined with TTL so that slots are not leaked

### Option B: session refs

Use /open_session and /close_session (already exist). But rather than use streaming session memory layout, still use HiCache and let the session hold a HiCache ref counter. 

In this case, the client would manually open/close session for every rollout, rather than keep one retention_slot across all rollouts which automatically clears previous rollouts.

### Related resources

## Related work

Streaming sessions (https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/19171) allow rollouts to be cleaned up as they finish. However, this is tied to a feature which is oriented around low-latency append-only sessions cached on-device. Our use case is different: we don't care about low-latency or avoiding Radix Cache and prefix matching, but we do care about throughput, utilization of HiCache, and non-append-only.

## Notes

Since sglang is agnostic to L3 backend and does not have an interface for evicting from L3, a solution for L3 may be nontrivial.
